All items being considered this evening are posted on the PPS website under the Board and Meetings tab. This meeting is also being streamed live on PPS YouTube page and will be replayed on Channel 28.

Let's see if the camera can see my shoes. I'm glad I wore my good shoes today. All right, good evening and welcome. Thank you, everyone, for being here. Sorry, I said that already. We are excited to be here at Grant High School. Tonight, we have a pretty full agenda. We have the following. We'll be receiving the local option levy report from the Community Budget Review Committee, an overview and the update on the racial equity and social justice support services strategy. We also be getting an update on the right sizing process, approving the extension of Superintendent Armstrong's contract. We'll be having a break at 7:20 to walk over to the Grant Bowl to celebrate the first home game that will be under the newly installed field lights.
Let's start off with the superintendent's report. Hand this over to Dr. Arksha.

Absolutely. Excited to be here on the fifth day of school. This will be quick because, really, the first week of school, or first few days of school, is about celebrating all of the children that we have in our buildings across Portland. So you have the wrong date on there, but I just wanted to show you a couple of faces of enthusiasm, excitement, cheer,

staff at work all the curiosity, and then, of course, the walking bus set to music. And speaking of music, the only thing that I have to share is a September celebration on September 15th, we'll have an Arts and Education Week celebration and a proclamation reading, and the date is on that slide for your review. That concludes the report. Thank you.
All right, next up, we have our report from our student represent to do, Sandel.

Hi, everybody. As we begin the school year, I wanted to say how excited I am for what's ahead. I know this year is going to bring both fun things and challenging things, but I am also looking forward to everything we will accomplish together as students, staff, and as a district. Another exciting part of beginning the school year is returning of fall sports. We are so excited to turn the lights on today at Grant, and I'm hoping that PPS brings home some state titles. At the same time, I know this school year will bring up difficult conversations, particularly around right-sizing and school closures. These are conversations that are never easy to have and can be very emotional. Schools are more than buildings, they are communities. Changes to them can have significant impacts on students, families, and staff. However, I also believe it's important that we are willing to have these conversations and think honestly about the future of our district. Right-sizing is ultimately about looking at how our schools, how our schools are running today,

and how student populations may change in the coming years, and how we can make sure that students have access to programs and opportunities that they deserve. We can not only look at this upcoming school year, we have to think about the years coming after it.

How are things going to change and how are we going to make it better? The decisions we make now have the potential to shape opportunities for students for many years to come. My hope is that through these difficult conversations, we focus on building a stronger and more successful future for every student in our district.

Thank you, Student Representative Rosendell. All right, next up, we have general public comment. First, we'll start with student comments and then move on to general. Before we begin, just want to share, review our guidelines for public comment. First, again, the board thanks you for taking the time to attend this meeting and providing your comments, public input, especially from our students, truly informs and improves our work. We look forward to hearing your thoughts and reflections. As board members, we are here to listen, not engage in conversation with those who are testifying. Our board office may follow up on board-related issues raised during public testimony. We also request that complaints about individual employees be directed to the superintendent's office as a personnel matter. I will also remind PPS staff who are giving public comments that they may not provide testimony about students that could violate confidentiality protections under FERPA. This includes testimony using information that could identify students, especially their school in their school community, by use of direct or indirect linkages such as school grade, special education, or other status. For materials you would like the board to receive, handouts, pictures,

etc., please email those to schoolboard at pps.net. When you begin, please clearly state your name and spell your last name. How many Ms. Powell do we have how many public commenters do we have today? We have twelve. 12. Alright, so you will have two minutes to speak. When you see the yellow light, that means you have 30 seconds to finish up your comment. And when the red light goes off, that means it's time. So let's start off with students. Ms. Powell, can you call up the first couple students?
We don't have any students signed up today.
All right, never mind then. All right, call up the first two on the list.
We have Jodi Shear and Rosie Boyer.

Good evening. My name is Jody Shearer, S-C-H-E-E-R. I'm a Portland native and a retired pediatrician with grandsons in PPS schools. Our kids are experiencing what I consider a public health emergency related to digital product overuse in school. I urge you to take action with the PDX Schools Before Screens model bills on intentional screen and AI use, in order to make urgent and significant progress in curbing screen time, digital pedagogies, and dangerous Internet access in our schools this year. To understand my urgency, please consider the following. Number one, the academic progress of Oregon's children continues to fall precipitously since 2019. We now rank at or near the bottom of all 50 states in reading and math in spite of last decade's 80% increase in education spending. Two, multitudes of studies have shown that screen overuse harms kids mentally, physically, emotionally, academically, and is totally preventable. Three, two-thirds of the time that kids spend on digital learning devices is wasted on entertainment and multitasking. Academic growth suffers due to these distractions, which decrease the focus and attention that kids need to learn. Four, finally, the equity gap in education has widened since the EdTech Revolution.

Black children are most likely to be harmed by screen time overuse, followed by low-income children. These kids spend 40 to 100 percent more time on screens each day than other kids and suffer disproportionately higher rates of academic failure and harms due to digital technologies. PPS families are asking school leaders to take urgent action to reverse course away from digital oversaturation in school. School leaders rapidly instituted one-to-one digital devices and pedagogy during the pandemic without careful scrutiny or vetting. In response to the proven widespread harm of digital technologies and overuse, the families of current school children are asking you to take urgent and immediate corrective action to protect our children now.
Thank you. Yes, thank you. If there's more on your public testimony that we'd like the board to read, please email it to us. Yes. Thank you. And this goes for everybody else, too. All right,

go for it. Hi, my name is Rosie Boyer, B-O-Y-E-R. My son attended King Elementary School. He's now an eighth grader at Tubman and will attend Jefferson last year. I'm encouraged by the district's stated focus on equity and improving the experience of historically underserved schools with the resizing process. As this process moves forward, my biggest concern is making sure that those principles remain central when we go from talking about goals to making decisions about individual schools. Some school communities have more time, money, connections, and experience organizing against change than others. Everyone deserves a voice, but the loudest or best resourced opposition cannot become what determines what schools are preserved. I hope the board will establish and publicly share a clear framework for how these decisions will be made before individual schools are proposed for closure. King is a good example for why that matters. It has one of the smallest attendance boundaries in PPS. Given how the little geographic area King is allowed to draw from, the fact that it maintains the enrollment it does shows how important the school is to its community. PPS has tried to enlarge King's boundary before, but strong opposition led the district to reverse course.

That is exactly why I worry about those voices that carry the most weight in this process. If we look only at King's enrollment without asking why its boundary is so small, we risk allowing past inequities to shape the next round of decisions, too. In north and northeast Portland, especially, today's enrollment patterns did not develop in a vacuum. Boundaries, segregation, displacement, and the ability of different communities to influence district decisions are all part of that history. I'm optimistic about this process. I hope we put the rules in place now before individual school communities are fighting for their own buildings so that equity remains what drives the hardest decisions. Thank you.
Thank you.

Shift andb Urellma have been collecting community complaints about criminal actions during bike rides and not reporting them to the police for nearly a decade now, per Shift to Bikes publicly stated anti-police cooperation policy. This and many shift uh bike rides are known as rolling dive bar, which means that participants openly consume alcohol, marijuana, and harder drugs before, during, and after the ride, including while on school grounds. I'm requesting that PPS work with the Portland police to create permanent trespass orders from all PPS properties against the current board members of Shift Bikes and their fiscal sponsor umbrella. at Abernethy Elementary around 7:30 p.m., while ride leaders approvingly observed. Please protect Portland schools and school children from these dangerous bike rides and dangerous bike community leaders. It only takes one intoxicated person dropping one of their bags to provide a trip that will ruin a child's life forever, and they don't even care. Responsible adults don't go to the playground to do their drugs. So why is this allowed in Portland? I'll be here all evening. Anybody if anybody has questions, I also have copies of the mandatory reporter complaint that I filed against shift to bikes. All right, take care. Bye. Thank you.

Hi, my name is Frances Chuning. I am a parent of an incoming kindergartner at Riki Elementary School. I'm also a member of Schools Beyond Screens. But tonight I'm here about the proposals to close schools. I am experiencing right now the joy of entering a neighborhood school. This is a school that has, my daughter, her first day, she walks in, she has friends from the neighborhood in all the grades. This school has institutional knowledge that's been learned and earned over the years from the staff from the PTA that can be passed on. I know we are not the only school like this. There are schools like this throughout the city. And a big concern of mine is the messaging that has come out about what size schools need to be to be successful. I read the Oregonian article where it was quoted that 360 is the threshold, 360 or more for elementary schools, and two teachers per grade. That means class sizes of 30 students. Now, this was referenced as being taken from the quality measurement, I forget the name right now. That is not what they said.

Their report said a good size for an elementary school is between 300 and 400. That was taken from a study that was done compiling research about what schools are most successful for students, I encourage you to read that report. That report is clear. That report is a cry saying research shows again and again, smaller schools are more successful for students, and in particular, for students of low socioeconomic background, students of ethnic minorities. It is a crucial element for equity. So I am very alarmed that people are saying 360 is a threshold we got from this report. It's simply not true, and that makes me not trust what the basis of decision-making is going on.
Thank you. Ms. Powell, can you call the next two?
Matt Coolidge and Ryan Lyle.

Hey there. My name is Matt Coolidge, and I'm a parent of a first grader at Riki Elementary School as well. My comments about the right-sizing process, which has felt rushed and incredibly opaque in its aims to date. There have been constantly moving goalposts. Last spring, 11 schools was the high end of projected closures, and now we're at 25. I would be surprised if that number didn't continue to creep higher as this process unfolds. It's clear that we're trying to build the plane as we fly it here, which hardly feels like the recipe for a successful outcome in public education. We understand there's a challenge with declining enrollment numbers, one that's certainly not unique to Portland. Closing schools is a drastic step with hugely negative repercussions, not only for impacted students, but for the communities that rally around and take pride in their local schools. We've seen failed right-sizing attempts play out repeatedly in other U.S. cities in recent years, yet, we are now choosing to barrel forward seemingly with the same playbook here in Portland, regardless of the clear consequences it poses. There is no scenario where you can credibly point to school closures as making Portland a more attractive destination for young families,

and this is at a time when the city desperately needs to attract more young families for its long-term growth and prosperity. I recognize our current path is not sustainable, but I'm far from convinced that right-sizing is the best or even only step we can take. We can't afford to get this critical decision wrong by charging headlong without a clearly articulated plan or even loose success metrics around class sizes or a clear commitment to what specific resources would be like in a post-right-sizing world. Instead of simply focusing on closing schools, I'd love to hear the school board's view on how we can better recruit more of the many, many unenrolled students in the district into PPS for a more sustainable future. Why not build bridges instead of destroy them? Thank you.
Thank you.

Hi there. I'm Ryan Lyle, R-I-O-N-L-Y-L-E. Unfortunately, I don't have such a nice presented or prepared speech. I'm a parent of kids at Winterhaven, which is a focused school, and I just wanted to make the case that when you guys decide on whatever criteria, I mean, I agree we shouldn't close schools, you know, if there's options. But I would just make the case for looking at schools that have a very high demand, like some focused option schools, lottery schools.

Because there's something, it's a data point that's saying that parents, families want to go to these schools. What is it about these schools that are so appealing to people? And I have a feeling that the choices that people have in our district allow people to make the decision to stay in the district rather than look for other options. Anyways, I appreciate it. It's a really hard thing you guys have to do, but just putting that out there for your criteria. Look at retention rates, look at wait lists, look at why people are traveling across the city to get their kids to some schools. Luckily, it's my neighborhood school. I'm there because it's a two-block walk for my kids. But, anyways, thanks so much. It's a hard thing you guys have to do.
Thank you. Ms. Powell, can you call the next two?
Next, we have James Powell and Kimberly Gwillick.

Live. My name is James Powell, P-O-W-E-L-L, and I have been a Winterhaven parent for seven years. I am not in the neighborhood, unfortunately. I go five miles to get there and have this whole time. And I want to convince you that Winter Haven is the most important school to keep open in this difficult right-sizing process. Winter Haven is a unique and intentional space where some of the city's most vulnerable children are given sanctuary, stability, and critical skills in STEAM. Its distinction starts from the top, where, unlike some schools, the principal keeps a steady hand on the tiller year after year for 17 years now. I verified that today. Principal San Diego is also popular with his staff, first hand, and that itself increases stability through retention. The level of retention of staff and teachers is wholly remarkable. This distinction then extends to the teachers who are 201 seriously dedicated to the success of the students. The STEAM curriculum is successful. I have a PhD in physics, and I can testify to the formidable reasoning powers in addition to math and science skills that the children acquire.

Unlike any other school I'm aware of, the Winter Haven Science Fair is mandatory for all students in K-8, which is certainly the best way to teach science. And finally, the lottery, which is constructed to give priority to kids who qualify for the free lunch program, gives access to this unique and successful community to the most poor and vulnerable children in the city. Please do not close Winterhaven. Thank you for listening.

Thank you. Good evening. My name is Kimberly Griltz, G-R-I-L-C, and I'm also a parent of a kindergartner at Winterhaven Elementary. My family recently returned to Portland from living abroad, and one of the most important decisions we made was finding the right school for our son. We specifically applied to Winterhaven because of its STEAM focus, and we were thrilled when he was accepted. My son is five years old, but he has already told us that he wants to be a builder or a fixer. He loves math, he loves building things, figuring out how things work, and taking things apart, making things. He also loves art. So when I learned about Winter Haven, I saw a school where these interests wouldn't have to exist separately from his education. They could come together as part of how he learns and explores the world. That's why I'm concerned about the possibility of school closures. I understand that PPS is facing difficult financial circumstances,

and I know there are no easy answers. But I hope the Board will look beyond the immediate question of which buildings can be closed and ask what kind of educational opportunities we want to preserve for Portland students. Charter schools and focused schools serve as an important purpose because children are not all motivated by or best served by exactly the same educational environment. Some students thrive in a particular academic focus, teaching model, school culture, or community. Having different options allows families to find an environment where their children can truly engage and thrive. And closing schools has consequences beyond losing a building. It can mean teacher and staff layoffs, larger class sizes, disrupted communities, and fewer choices for families. And as also an educator myself, I understand the implications of those types of layoffs and larger class sizes, too. I want to also be candid that if Winter Haven were to close, our family would have to seriously reconsider whether PPS remains the right choice for our son. We came back to Portland, chose PPS and Winter Haven, and were fortunate enough to find a school that feels like an exceptional match for our child. Thank you. Thank you.
Is that it? Can I bring in some virtual people? Sam, Sam Bulick.

Hello. My name is Sam Bulick, B-U-L-L-I-C-K. I'll be adding my hat into the ring as a Winter Haven parent. I'm also a pulmonary and critical care physician, and I'm covering right now, but don't worry, there's another physician that's covering. On behalf of Winterhaven families, we recognize that PPS faces serious financial and enrollment challenges and we support responsible right-sizing. We hope that a focus of this campaign We hope that a focus of this campaign is supporting and protecting programs that families are actively choosing. Winterhaven is a district-wide K through H STEAM program that is highly successful and, as a result, has demonstrated high demand through the PPS lottery system, like we've already heard, including substantial waitlist demand in recent years. Closing Winter Haven may reduce a building from the district's inventory, but it will also eliminate a program that helps retain families and PPS, like we've already heard. Winterhaven should not be eliminated, but should be replicated to draw families and students back into PPS. Build bridges,

don't destroy them like we just heard. Before making any decision, we asked the board to evaluate Winterhaven based on total educational and financial value, not simply building utilization. What equivalent STEAM K through 8 program would replace Winterhaven? We are not asking PPS to ignore its financial realities, we are asking the district to make decisions based on complete data and to protect programs that families actively choose. Thank you.
Thank you.

Yes, thank you. Hi, good evening. My name is Chelsea Reardon. I am from the elementary school Riki. I'm like honored to be joining it this year with my kindergartner. I went to Portland Public Schools and then moved all over the country for a large number of years and was really excited to move back to Portland and raise my family here. I am so passionate about small, tight-knit, close, like close community schools. And so I was amazed to be part of Riki and welcomed by the PTA and the principal, and it's been amazing so far. So I was kind of heartbroken when all the right-sizing started happening, and lots of talk of it. And I guess what I want to know is: what exactly will right-sizing be? What exactly is it going to provide for our students? What exactly are the benefits of it? I'm not ignoring that there is such an economical problem right now and a huge burden. However, I truly believe that our kids deserve everything, and I think that if you're really short-sighted about this,

that you're going to lose more and more families. I also think transparency would be asked of the board and of this whole process because there, like mentioned earlier, there have been some discrepancies about like the QEM requirements or like the recommendations for how many teachers to students there are, and I just feel like the more and more we're hearing about this, the less trustworthy it's becoming. And I just ask that you look into the future where there are families that do want to come to PPS and are excited about it and passionate about it. And I think that massive closures are not the way to go. And I really ask you, like, what other initiatives have we tried yet? And I know that Riki district personally is going to be increasing their total units by one hundred and or more in the next coming years. And so I just don't understand the short-sightedness of it. We have incoming families potentially coming, but where are they going to go? And so I just beg you to reconsider your votes on this when the time comes.
Thank you.

Again, if you there's more to your testimony that you did not get to say, you are always feel free to email that to the board at schoolboard at pps.net. So, thank you, everyone who came today to testify, and there's also some more later, so we'll get there. All right, next up, we have comments from our union partners. I believe we have the Portland Association of Teachers President, Alicia Chavez, here to provide comments. Thank you again for coming today.

Hello, good evening. I don't have to introduce myself. I feel like I know everybody here. I'm going to be very direct and use some language that I use in my classroom that I am definitely feeling in the yellow/slash red zone today. Educators and school staff have been told year after year to make sacrifices. We have endured some of the largest furlough cuts. We have watched our coworkers lose their jobs, and now you are threatening to close up to 20 schools. But I want you to understand what that actually means. Educators are already starting the school year with huge caseloads and enormous class sizes. Teachers are being asked to meet the needs of more students with fewer adults, fewer resources and less time. Specialists and core enrichment educators are carrying caseloads that are already unsustainable, and some are even split between multiple schools. Special education teachers do not even have enough minutes in their day to meet student needs on an IEP, with some caseloads as large as 45. Counselors, social workers and other school staff are being stretched beyond what is reasonable. And now you're talking about closing schools and moving even more students into fewer buildings. Those class sizes will get bigger.

Those caseloads will get bigger. The pressure on educators will get worse. And our students will ultimately pay the price. So, explain to me how this is a financial crisis when we're talking about classrooms, but somehow there is money when we're talking about a superintendent's contract. This This proposal increases the superintendent's total compensation to well over $400,000 by the 28-29 school year. It increases the retirement contributions, it increases the monthly vehicle allowance, it increases the vacation cash out, and it creates retention bonuses that can reach 5% of base salary every year. Meanwhile, educators are being told every day. Last year, take furlough days, volunteer your time constantly, accept layoffs, take more students, take bigger classes, do more with less, and now we're supposed to accept that closing schools is somehow part of the solution. Let's be honest about what's happening. You cannot close schools without increasing the pressure on the schools that remain,

you cannot eliminate classrooms and expect students to just disappear. They don't disappear. They get moved, they get absorbed in different places, and the educators who remain that weren't laid off in the process are expected to somehow make it work. We've heard that the superintendent's compensation is comparable to other districts, but I will also say the other districts you are looking at have smaller management teams in comparison. But let's talk about educator salaries, right? Because we're doing comparisons. Evergreen pays more. They have a higher top of the scale for educators. Beaverton pays more. They have a higher top of the scale for teachers. But PPS educators aren't constantly looking across the river or over Highway twenty six and asking themselves who will pay me more. They stay because they are committed to Portland students, right? They stay because they believe in our schools. They stay because they believe in our community. And I expect the same for our superintendent, and frankly, I expect the same for you all as our board. And let me be clear about something else. I expect to see the same energy that I'm going to see today when we go into bargaining this year.

Is there money to retain and compensate for leadership? Then I expect this board to bring that same level of urgency, creativity, and commitment to the bargaining table for educators who educate Portland's children every single day. Don't tell us that the district can't afford meaningful investments in educators while approving significant increases at the top. Don't tell us that there is no money for competitive compensation, manageable workloads, and the conditions educators need to stay in this district and students while approving raises, increased benefits, and retention bonuses for the superintendent while maintaining the status quo cabinet of direct reports to her. We will remember the choices you make when we sit across the bargaining table from you all. Because educators deserve to know: will the same standard apply to us? Will you all just fight just as hard to retain educators? Will you fight just as hard to retain school staff when you're looking at a $65 million deficit? And will you invest in reducing class sizes and caseloads? Will you invest in keeping experienced educators in Portland? Or will the financial crisis suddenly become the reason you tell educators they need to accept less? Because we have seen this movie before and we don't like it. We are asked to sacrifice while those at the top are protected. This is not shared sacrifice,

and it is not sustainable. You are talking about closing neighborhood schools while increasing executive compensation. You are talking about huge class sizes and impossible caseloads while increasing executive compensation. You are telling families that their neighborhood schools may disappear while telling the superintendent that now is the right time for increased benefits and retention bonuses. That is not the message Portland students, families, and educators need to hear. That's not what they deserve. Our standard should not be what is the most we can pay. Our standard should be what is the best for Portland students right now. And how we can fight to get them everything they need to be successful adults. If we're in a financial crisis, which we are, every dollar matters. And if every dollar matters, then this board needs to explain why additional executive compensation should take priority over keeping schools open, keeping educators employed, reducing class sizes, and making caseloads manageable. Because educators can't continue absorbing all of that, every cut, while leadership is protected from any kind of consequence.

We are already carrying the weight, and it's exhausting, and you are asking us to carry even more. Bigger classes, bigger caseloads, more students displaced by school closures, more instability, more work, and then you're asking us to watch the superintendent get a raise. We are in a financial crisis, so everyone needs to share that sacrifice. Not just educators, not just school staff, not just students and families, everybody. Portland educators have shown you our priorities, and our priorities are always Portland students. And honestly, how many times do I have to say the same thing over and over again. I kind of want to keep a tally. And I have heard from our previous presidents year after year saying the same thing, too. So I'm asking: when will you start to actually understand that this is educators' reality and actually do something.

Because right now, it looks like we only remember we're in a financial crisis when it's time to cut classrooms, close schools, lay off educators, or bargain with the people who are doing the work. And that's not the leadership I want to see.

And this year, because the budget report window was so small, we had to separate those processes. The CBRC, I know we have may have some members. I see Angela Benia, thank you for your service. We did have to reconvene that committee to talk about the methodology in which the district identifies the eligible expenditures under the local option levy, and we were able to come forward with an agreement that that methodology is indeed solid and worthy of certification. So, in your packet, you have a copy of the review and report, and just note that this is for the 24-25 fiscal year. And with that, I'm happy to answer any questions you might have.
All right, Bart. If there's any questions, now's the time to ask.
I just have. Go ahead, Dr. Slick.

I just wanted to. Oh, sorry. Into the void, I just wanted to say thanks for the consideration. I didn't have any questions, it was clearly written, understandable, and I was just really grateful that they did the work of reviewing it. And the lack of questions isn't because of a lack of value.
Yeah, we definitely appreciate the extra time that the committee was able to give to this. And thank you, Director Sullivan, for your leadership with the group.

Yes, this year, the group was really committed and spending that extra time to do this, trying to find everybody a time to get together was quite interesting. But they really pulled it together. Very much appreciated.
I don't know if it's maybe it's a question and comment.

So, this year, or last year, I guess last school year, the the levy fund collected a total of 104.4 million revenue and how does that comp do you remember how that compares to the previous years? It looks like, if I remember correctly, it looks like it went down.
Yes, it was down about $5 million and did contribute to our 25-26 year shortfall.

Great., thank you That's exactly what I was like. And then again, I'm just stating for the record. Last year the levy was able to fund 741 teachers, but the future expectation is 686, or sorry, 686. Yes. Yes, I remember, yeah, it used to be even higher than 741 when it was first passed. So I think, yeah. And then I guess the other, this may be for later, but the cap that the state imposes on levy funds is set at it was set at a percentage of the general fund, right? I can't remember what it was. It would have been like 116-ish million.
Yeah. Okay.

Yeah. The reason the local option levy collection was lower this year was due to the compression that happened in the downtown areas. We had our county economists come and visit with you guys about the dynamics that are impacting the levy and kind of the outlook for the levy. So, further in the report, you can see that in five years, if we're still lucky enough to have the same level of lev local option support, that it would be fund perhaps 25% fewer positions than currently. So, if we stay on trend with expenses and our revenue staying flat.

And then, if we're looking at in the future of raising the levy amount the moment you hit that cap, $116 million-ish, well, current, based on the current budget, right? What happens to the money that's raised over that cap?
It's retained in the system, it's just remains uncollected.
So it goes back to the state?
